content.title: About
content.content: Scallops are bivalve mollusks from the family Pectinidae. When baked or broiled, they are cooked at high heat, preserving their tender texture and sweet, slightly briny flavor. They are commonly served as an appetizer or incorporated into main dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scallops can grow rapidly; some species double their weight in just a few weeks.
In the wild, scallops filter water, helping to keep marine environments clean.
There are over 300 species of scallops, but the Atlantic sea scallop (Placopecten magellanicus) is most common in cuisine.
Scallops can clap their shells together using powerful adductor muscles, a behavior that also helps them escape predators.
Baking often includes butter, garlic, cheese, or breadcrumbs to add flavor and crispness.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Scallops provide complete protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nerve function and the formation of red blood cells.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many seafood options, scallops contain very little saturated fat.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s promote heart health and help reduce inflammation.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Scallops can accumulate toxins and heavy metals from polluted waters; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: While moderate, the cholesterol in scallops should be considered by those with high cholesterol.

items.title: Need for thorough cooking
items.content: Raw scallops may harbor harmful bacteria; cook until shells fully open to ensure safety.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked scallops are served hot, often drizzled with lemon, butter, garlic, or topped with grated cheese. They can be added to pasta, risotto, salads, or enjoyed as a standalone appetizer. Avoid overcooking to keep them moist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh scallops should be kept in the refrigerator in a tightly sealed container, covered with a damp cloth, and used within 24 hours. Frozen scallops store at –18 °C for up to 3–4 months. Rinse under cold running water before cooking.
